newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Environment council short on proposals for decision.
newsitem.headline: Environment council short on proposals for decision.

text.p: Tuesday's Environment Council looks likely to be similar to many of the other Luxembourg Councils so far this month in that there is little or nothing up for a decision.
Ministers are due to begin discussions with an orientation debate on the European Commission's proposal to review the fifth framework action programme for the environment "Towards Sustainability".
A common position by the December Council is one of the Irish presidency's main environment aims for its time in office.
"We have done quite alot of work on it in the working group. There areno major problems just lots and lots of minor ones," said an Irish diplomat.
The focus on Tuesday will be on the integration of environment issues into other EU policy areas, broadening the range of available instruments and discussing implementation.
The proposal is for a Council decision rather than a Commission work programme, meaning that it will not contain many specific targets or dates for any particular action to be completed.
"It's a review of the programme not a new programme. We think it's important to get it done quickly. This was supposed to have been done by the end of 1995," the diplomat added.

The next item, namely preparation for the third conference of the parties on the convention on biodiversity, is unlikely to set off any fireworks. One EU diplomat said most points for the Buenos Aires meeting next month were largely procedural, in contrast with last year's more substantial agenda in Jakarta.

Ireland's second common position hope, on the Commission proposal to modify Directive 90/219 on the contained use of genetically modified organisms (GMOs), comes up for its second appearance in Council.

The proposal suggests changing the scope of Directive 90/219, altering the committee procedures for technical amendment, changing the risk categorisation and the administrative procedures and further specifying required containment and control measures.
It would abolish the different regulatory treatment for research laboratories and industrial ones.

Presidency questions to ministers include asking whether definitions for micro-organisms and GMOs are sufficiently precise and whether the proposed classification of contained uses, based on risk assessment, is the best way to identify the optimum containment measures.

The Irish also want to hear what ministers think about increasing the administrative requirements on GMO researchers on the basis of increased assessed risk and whether the four proposed risk categories are appropriate.

"The intention is to discuss the main articles to make sure the presidency is going in the right direction. Definition of the scope, definition of the four different classes of contained use and the article on what notification procedures should take place," the diplomat said.
The Dutch, Danes and Swedes have problems with the approach, the diplomat said, adding that for the Dutch the text was not deregulatory enough while for the other two, it was not tight enough.
"Everbody else is pretty much in favour of what the presidency is proposing," the diplomat said.

Next up is likely to be the public session, scheduled to take place between 1200 (1000 GMT) and 1330 (1130 GMT), on the Commission communication and proposals COM(96)248 for car emissions and fuel quality directives.
Ministers will read out their positions in response to these proposals and to three questions drafted by the permanent representatives' committee.

These are whether the proposals are in line with the motor vehicle emissions policy foreseen by Directive 94/12/EC, whether the standards proposed for 2000 are acceptable and what should be the elements to consider for the proposed next stage.

While open debates at Environment Councils have proved fairly sterile in the past, the significance of these Auto/Oil programme proposals, and the controversy they have sometimes stirred up, is such that Tuesday's affair may throw up something more interesting.
Cameras are then switched off for ministers to turn their attention to questions related to the Commission's proposal for a review of the Community strategy for waste management, COM(96)399.

These include whether harmonised terminology for waste definition be central to the review, what actions should fall to the Community, member states and waste operators, what refinements are required to the policy and whether efforts should be made to promote markets for recycled products.

More controversial are questions on the concept of producer responsibility versus shared responsibility -- the former backed by the Commission -- on how far waste should be shipped before treatment and whether countries should deal with their own wastes rather than export or import them.
These last two refer particularly to waste exports from Germany to countries such as Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and even Finland, according to the same diplomat.
Another orientation debate awaits ministers on the Commission's proposal COM(94)612 for changes to the drinking water Directive 80/778.

Questions here are whether proposed derogations will solve the problems of non-compliance while protecting public health, what to do about lead levels and the acceptability of the Commission proposal to retain the limit on allowed concentrations of individual pesticides and to abolish the cumulative limit.

There is a further question relating to the Commission suggestions for preventing trade barriers in respect to drinking water in food, as a piped commodity across borders and as bottled mineral water.
On another topic, ministers are also due to discuss the follow-up to June's conference on climate change and prepare the EU position for protocol negotiations.

The European Environment Agency reported in September that "considerable uncertainty" surrounded the prospects for EU countries to meet their pledges to stabilise their carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions at 1990 levels by the year 2000.
What was more, the EEA added, current EU measures were insufficient to prevent further increases in carbon dioxide after 2000.

"If the EU wants to achieve its targets of avoiding adverse effects, an accelerated policy is needed. A reduction in the range of at least 30 to 50 percent of all greenhouse gases might be needed in industrialised countries (inlcuding the EU) by 2010 compared to 1990 levels, depending on the expectations for the range of emissions in developing countries," it said.

Environment ministers are also due to hear a report related to proposal COM(95)737 for a Council regulation amending Council Regulation (EEC) No 3254/91 prohibiting the use of leghold traps in the Community and on the import of pelts of animals which are caught using methods defined as inhumane by international rules.
They are likely to hear reports on any progress made during this week's talks in Russia's St Petersburg between officials from the Commission, Russia, Canada and the United States.

Among the any-other-business points are two from the Commission, on genetically modified maize and on the implementation of the Habitats Directive, one from Britain on atmospheric ozone pollution and another from the Austrians on taxing kerosene.
